title: Breaking Through With Tactics!! | King's India Defense | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: White plays g3 — the Fianchetto Variation, a hugely reputable line chosen by many grandmasters against both the King's Indian and the Grünfeld, famously recommended in Avrukh's '1.d4'.
A crossroads: a Grünfeld player must seize this moment to play d5, because if you castle White develops the queen's knight to c3 and takes d5 away, forcing you into a King's Indian.
We commit to a King's Indian, putting the pawn on d6 rather than d5 — even after the knight to c3 prevents d5, that's fine, it's what we want.
The point of routing the knight to d7 was to prepare e5, which we now play, striking at the centre.
The flexible c6 is a common multipurpose King's Indian move — it controls squares and, semi-tactically, opens the d8-a5 diagonal for the queen.

And there's the idea — the queen to a5. It's not that a5 itself is special; it's a safe jumping-off point, very hard to attack and out of the other pieces' way, from which the queen can swing to b4 to hit c4 or drop back as needed. White's sharpest reply is the queen to c2 — the instinctive bishop to d2 actually cuts White's own queen's contact with d4.
teaches: the queen as a flexible hub

moves.spoken: Now discharge the central tension with the capture on d4 — wait too long and White closes the centre, leaving our rook biting on granite.
Recapturing with the queen would walk it into a discovery, so the knight recapture is the natural, sound choice.
The rook to e8 is flexible and full of tactical venom, leaning on the e4-pawn — revealing less than jumping the knight out immediately.

The knight jumps to e5, its main King's Indian post — the c5-square is awkward here with the queen on a5. This c4-and-e4 structure is a Maróczy-like bind: White has a big space advantage, and a King's Indian player must be willing to sit in cramped positions.

The King's Indian is an anti-engine opening — engines love White's space and overrate the edge, but the positions are hard to play practically. Since d5 will never happen, we nibble around the edges instead: a6 is a low-risk move preparing b5 to chew at the c4-pawn. Nothing happens fast here; it's a long maneuvering battle where you accumulate weaknesses, hedgehog-style, until something gives.
teaches: create weaknesses for the long run

moves.spoken: When White plays the queen to d2, spot the forkable squares — his queen and king now sit on a fork pattern, and our own queen is in an undefended standoff to watch. The f3-square is the target.

So c5 chases the knight — positionally committal, weakening d5, but in the service of a tactic: once the knight moves, the bishop takes on h3, winning a pawn and, crucially, deflecting White's fianchetto bishop to crack open the centre.
teaches: commit a pawn for a tactic

moves.spoken: The bishop crashes on h3 — untouchable, because the knight jumps to f3 with check, forking king and queen and winning the queen for two minor pieces. A classic textbook deflection sacrifice: even if White declines, we've traded off the fianchetto bishop that holds his centre together.

When it gets chaotic, break the position into its parts. Rather than flirt with a fatally weak king after giving up our own fianchetto bishop, the Russian-schoolboy choice is the knight takes e4 — steering into a clean, better endgame of a rook and three pawns against two minor pieces.

After the knight grabs e4 our queen is hanging from the standoff, so we must take White's queen — the tactic we spotted the moment the queens faced off. At this level, above 2000, there's simply more to calculate: the pieces are better placed, the openings more principled, so visualisation becomes everything.

Converting: keep the one truly open file, don't hand back material just to dodge a check, and expand on the kingside step by step with the king and pawns — always watching for forks, which decide these games. A neat safety habit in time pressure: park your rook on the opposite colour to the enemy bishop so you can't blunder it.
